Sign up for free Δ Support for Prop. 1 is vast, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, the state Democratic party, home-sharing company AirBnB, major unions and more. Want more? Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. NO on Prop. 1
Called the “Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026,” this is $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds with only $1.25 billion allocated to benefit veterans. The rest will finance other housing assistance programs. Bonds are borrowed money. Like all general obligation bonds, the actual cost to taxpayers will be roughly double the advertised amount due to interest that must be paid to investors. Bonds are the most expensive way to pay for anything, and when used to pay for programs instead of capital projects, it’s a much greater burden on taxpayers than just paying for these programs from the budget.
Vote NO on 1 .
NO on Prop. 2
This measure makes changes to the Gann Limit, passed by voters in 1979, and to the rules for the Budget Stabilization Account (“Rainy Day Fund”) that were approved by voters in 2014. Tax revenue goes up and down in California with the stock market, because of the state’s dependence on taxes from high earners and capital gains. Proposition 2 attempts to address this revenue volatility challenge with new rules for the Budget Stabilization Account. However, while Prop. 2 addresses the treatment of appropriations into and out of reserve funds in a way that makes sense from the perspective of addressing revenue volatility, it doesn’t address the weakening of the Gann Limit by Propositions 98 (1988) and 111 (1990), enabling reckless overspending that has led to structural deficits and self-inflicted budget “emergencies.” California is in desperate need of fiscal discipline. The changes in the state constitution that permit unlimited spending should be reversed. Prop. 2 falls far short of real spending reform and, unfortunately, amounts to little more than a Band-Aid on a severed limb.
Vote NO on 2 .
NO on Prop. 3
Remember the “temporary” income tax rate hike “for the schools” that was passed in 2012 and “temporarily” renewed in 2016? This measure renews it again and this time makes it permanent. California has the highest income tax rates in the nation, and every year the state has a bigger budget and a higher cost of living to show for it. These “temporary” income tax rate hikes should not be a backdoor method for permanent tax increases.
Vote NO on 3 .
NO on Prop. 4
Existing law, the Political Reform Act of 1974 (PRA), prohibits the use of tax money to finance political campaigns for elective office. Proposition 4 would remove that ban. HJTA has previously won court cases upholding this provision of the PRA, and we haven’t changed our position. Taxpayers should not have to pay the campaign expenses of candidates running for office or incumbents running for re-election.
Vote NO on 4 .
NO on Prop. 5
This measure alters the constitutional right to recall a state officer and vote for a replacement candidate. Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate in recalls of statewide officeholders and state legislators. Offices would be filled by appointment or later special election. If a governor was recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would become Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term or until a special election, depending on timing. Proposition 5 allows the recalled officeholder to run in the special election to fill the seat, which current law prohibits. This measure makes a mockery of the recall process.
Vote NO on 5 .
NO on Prop. 37
This measure authorizes $25 billion in bonds for a program that would offer second-mortgage loans for down payments on newly constructed or converted homes (not existing homes) to eligible buyers who earn less than 200% of the area median income. Although there is no direct cost to taxpayers, a market downturn could cause mass foreclosures if stretched borrowers are unable to make their payments or sell the home for what they owe. Investors bear the financial risks, but the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) must manage this massive pool of funds to protect the bondholders and pay them the interest they are owed. HJTA appreciates the intent of this measure, but we have concerns about the size of the program and the criteria for eligibility to participate. Prop. 37 is not a constitutional amendment, which leaves it subject to legislative alteration. More fundamentally, California’s housing crisis is better addressed with less government impediments to building rather than a new government program. We urge a No vote.
Vote NO on 37 .
NO on Prop. 38
Another bond measure, Proposition 38 authorizes $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for research and therapies related to using the body’s immune system to treat disease. There is no reason that this cost should be borne by California taxpayers. Viable research can be funded by pharmaceutical companies, foundations and the federal government. An analysis by CalMatters reveals that the ballot language criteria were tailored in a way that very likely excludes all but one institute in the entire state: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose prominent donor and co-founder is the chief backer of the proposition. Prop. 38 appears to be a clear case of self-dealing at the expense of taxpayers.
Vote NO on 38 .
YES on Prop. 39
Proposition 39 is the Voter ID initiative. While 36 states currently require some form of voter ID, California isn’t one of them. Voter ID is used successfully around the country to prevent voter impersonation at the polls and to ensure that mail ballots are validly submitted by eligible voters. It’s especially important to California taxpayers to secure our elections from the potential for fraud, because billions of dollars of tax measures are on the ballot in nearly every election.
Vote YES on 39 .
NO on Prop. 40
This is the “wealth tax,” supposedly affecting only billionaires but in fact a threat to every California taxpayer and homeowner. Proposition 40 imposes a “one-time tax” of 5% of “covered assets” valued above $1 billion. However, the measure includes language that allows the Legislature to rewrite the law later, potentially changing the thresholds, the assets that are covered, the percentage to be taken, and the number of times the tax would be levied. This is an entirely new type of tax, and we don’t know where it will lead. Will all Californians have to submit forms to the Franchise Tax Board declaring their assets every year? How much will ordinary Californians have to pay for “wealth tax preparation” to comply with this law?
Vote NO on 40 .
YES on Prop. 41
This measure requires pre-election audits of programs that would be funded by new statewide special taxes. It’s a good idea to find out where the existing funds are going before voters are asked to approve higher taxes for the same programs.
Vote YES on 41 .
YES on Prop. 42
In direct opposition to the “wealth tax,” this measure would prohibit any new state tax that taxes the ownership or control of personal property or applies retroactively based on activities or status that existed before the effective date of the new state tax. This will protect Californians, especially homeowners, from the risk of a “wealth tax” on the value of homes or any other accumulated savings and investments.
Vote YES on 42 .
YES on Prop. 43
Proposition 43 is the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 . It restores Prop. 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes. Prop. 43 closes the court-created “Upland” loophole that has allowed special interest groups to write their own tax increases, direct the money to themselves, collect signatures to place them on the ballot and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Because of this loophole, Californians are paying billions of dollars in taxes that they should not have had to pay.
Vote YES on 43 and tell a friend!
NO on Prop. 44
This measure requires community clinics that provide primary care to medically underserved areas and populations to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient services, not management and overhead. It authorizes the Attorney General to publish guidance on qualifying expenditures and lets the Department of Public Health issue waivers. It authorizes monetary penalties and criminal charges. It is sponsored by a powerful labor organization seeking to expand its control over private clinics.
Vote NO on 44 .
YES on Prop. 45
Few things have impeded rational housing policy in the state more than the California Environmental Quality Act. It slows down development which, in turn, limits housing supply, increasing the cost of living. Far from being a tool to address legitimate environment concerns, it has been used more frequently as leverage by labor organizations to exact favorable labor agreements. While CEQA reform to prevent excessive delays is necessary, Proposition 45 is not perfect since it carves out only certain projects for reform and locks in costly labor agreements. It also creates opportunities for government to pick winners and losers. But while HJTA would prefer a full revamp of CEQA, Prop. 45 is a good first step.
Vote YES on 45 .
LOCAL BALLOT MEASURE RECOMMENDATIONS
City of Los Angeles
NO on Measure FD
This is a one-half percent sales tax increase in the city of L.A. with the revenue earmarked for the fire department. We oppose this measure because the sales tax in Los Angeles will already rise to 10.25% in October because of Measure ER passing in L.A. County in June, and because the City Council and the Mayor should fully fund the fire department from the existing budget of approximately $15 billion without a tax increase. This measure is a special tax that should require a two-thirds vote to pass, but courts have allowed “citizens’ initiative tax increases,” placed on the ballot by collecting signatures, to pass with fewer votes. HJTA’s ballot measure, the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 (Proposition 43 on the November ballot) will close the loophole, but this tax increase, if approved by just 50% plus one vote, will squeeze through it before Proposition 43 takes effect in January.
City of Santa Monica
NO on Measure ES
This is a parcel tax, an extra $495 per taxable parcel of property every year, adjusted annually for inflation. The revenue is earmarked for schools. Special taxes are required by the constitution to be approved by two-thirds of voters, but this is another “citizens’ initiative tax increase” rushing to squeeze through the court-created “Upland” loophole before voters approve Proposition 43 in November.
City of Palos Verdes Estates
NO on Measure PVE
This is a renewal of a parcel tax with a massive increase in the per-parcel rate from $342 to $1,025 to pay for police services and “to pay down the City's unfunded accrued pension liability.” City voters previously rejected a different measure in June to renew and increase the temporary parcel tax.
El Dorado County
NO on Measure S
Measure S is a 30-year countywide sales tax increase. It would raise the sales tax by 3/8 percent. Marshall Medical Center is sponsoring the campaign for the tax. The Yes on S website states that “Marshall receives revenue to support $125M in bond issuance to fund capital improvements.” El Dorado County has only two hospitals: Marshall Medical Center and Barton Memorial Hospital. Measure S is structured so Marshall qualifies for the hospital funding while Barton does not. South Lake Tahoe residents would still pay the countywide tax even though Barton falls below the measure’s hospital eligibility threshold.
Five-County Bay Area
NO on regional transit sales tax
This is a sales tax increase of at least one-half percent (1% in San Francisco) in five Bay Area counties (San Francisco, Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, Santa Clara) to fund transit. Critics rightly argue that the longstanding financial and management problems of transit systems in the Bay Area will not be fixed with another tax increase. Beyond that, a higher sales tax burdens people who already pay high sales taxes and are struggling with the high cost of living. This measure, too, is a “citizens’ initiative tax increase” attempting to get through the court-created loophole before HJTA closes it with Proposition 43.

Full Crosstabs–Likely Voters Only
Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos KnowledgePanel. Interviews were conducted in
English and Spanish according to the respondents’ preferences. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. Interviewing took place
from October 16—22, 2026.
These crosstabs are based on a subgroup of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error, taking design effects from weighting into consideration, is ±3.8
percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups
is larger. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording,
question order, and survey timing.

Here’s what $44 billion would buy by Mikhail Zinshteyn (https://calmatters.org/author/mikhailzinshteyn/) October 24, 2026 Updated October 25, 2026 Republish Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Construction in a residential area that was burned during the Eaton Fire in 2025, in Altadena, on Aug. 3, 2026. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Sign up for free Δ Support for Prop. 1 is vast, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, the state Democratic party, home-sharing company AirBnB, major unions and more. Want more? Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists. The problem underlying California’s housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or — in the case of affordable housing — public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.

Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.

# Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.
## Summary
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance.
**Fiscal Impact**: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond.
**Supporters:** US Vets; CA Federation of Teachers; Self-Help for the Elderly; Habitat for Humanity CA; CA Alliance of Child & Family Services **Opponents:** None submitted

The problem underlying California’s housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or — in the case of affordable housing — public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.

Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.

The problem underlying California’s housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or — in the case of affordable housing — public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.

Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.

The problem underlying California’s housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or — in the case of affordable housing — public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.

Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.

Put on the Ballot by the Legislature

YES

NO

ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 1 builds affordable homes for veterans, seniors, people with disabilities, low- and middle-income working families, vulnerable Californians and essential workers-teachers, firefighters and nurses. Expands homeownership opportunities, fast-tracks affordable shovel-ready homes, helps those one crisis away from homelessness. Requires strict fiscal accountability and public oversight with no new taxes.
CON

Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Authorizes Bonds For Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.
Additional Titles
Cali fornia Proposition 1, Veteran and Housing Assistance Programs Bond Measure
Summary
Proposition 1 is a legislatively referred bond measure which was passed by the California Legislature on June 26, 2026, through Senate Bill 417 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) (SB 417). Both the Assembly and Senate votes exceeded the two-thirds majority required for the Legislature to place a bond measure before voters. Because legislatively referred bond measures also require the governor’s approval, Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signature on SB 417 completed the process of placing Proposition 1 on the ballot.
Proposition 1 would allow California to sell $11.25 billion through state bonds for housing programs. Of that amount, $10 billion would go toward housing assistance for low- and moderate-income Californians that would be repaid by the General Fund, while $1.25 billion would support the state’s home loan program for veterans.
The $10 billion for housing would fund a range of projects, including affordable rental housing, assistance for first-time homebuyers, farmworker and student housing, housing infrastructure, tribal housing projects, and local pilot programs aimed at lowering housing costs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The state would repay the $10 billion housing portion from the General Fund, at an estimated cost of $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Veterans participating in the loan program would repay their home loans to the state. These payments are then used to pay back the bonds.
Because the state has to pay interest when it borrows money, the bond would cost about 15 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the projects up front with money the state already has.
What your vote means (LAO's Analysis)
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing programs for income-qualified Californians.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not issue the proposed $11.25 billion in bonds for low-income housing programs.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents argue that California’s housing affordability and homelessness crises require substantial public investment and that Proposition 1 would directly improve the lives of people struggling to find or keep stable housing. They contend that funding affordable housing construction and preservation, homeownership assistance, and housing for veterans, farmworkers, students, and homeless and foster youth would provide meaningful help to Californians most affected by high housing costs.
Opponents argue that California should not take on additional debt for housing when the state has substantial revenues and could fund these programs directly. They contend that the underlying housing problem is a shortage of available homes caused largely by regulations and development restrictions, rather than a lack of government spending on affordable housing.

Quick overview: Proposition 1
LAist's AirTalk host Larry Mantle's ballot cram session gets you ready to vote with guests Michael Alvarez, of Caltech, Sara Sadhwani of Pomona College, and Lee E. Ohanian of UCLA and the Hoover Institution.
This measure asks voters to approve $11.25 billion in state bonds for various affordable housing strategies. The revenue would go toward the construction of new income-restricted apartments, supportive housing for tenants overcoming homelessness, mortgage assistance for veterans and a number of other programs.
What’s at stake?
According to recent U.S. Census Bureau statistics (https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48945), about 54% of California renters officially qualify as “cost-burdened,” meaning they pay more than 30% of their income on rent. The only states with higher levels of rent burden are Florida and Nevada.
California needs to build about 1 million new homes (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/affordable-housing-units-setback-california) specifically for low-income residents, based on current statewide planning goals. Proposition 1 aims to speed up that process by raising money from bonds that would be repaid from the state’s general fund over the next 25 years.
Official title on the ballot: Prop. 1: Authorizes bonds for housing affordability programs
Language you will see (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/index.htm) on the ballot:
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. Fiscal Impact : Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond.
What your vote means
A "yes" vote means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
A "no" vote means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
Understanding Prop. 1
Affordable housing units generally set rents at no more than 30% of a tenant’s income. That means they often do not generate enough rental income to be profitable for developers. That’s where public subsidies come in.
In recent years, California has put more funding toward creating low-cost housing. According to a recent state legislative analysis (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billAnalysisClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), California has funded various affordable housing programs with $8 billion from the state’s general fund since 2019.
But some of those funding streams are now drying up.
A previous measure also called Proposition 1, passed by voters in 2018, approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable housing and veteran mortgage programs. Proposition 2, also from 2018, put $2 billion toward the creation of 7,000 supportive units for formerly unhoused tenants. Both funds are now depleted.
Those state funds have run out at a time when state lawmakers say California can no longer rely on Washington, D.C., to expand or continue federal affordable housing efforts. They argue Prop. 1 could make an immediate difference for an estimated 45,000 units that are in the construction pipeline but have yet to break ground due to a lack of gap financing.
Here’s what supporters say
In addition to helping low-income renters, formerly unhoused tenants and veterans, Proposition 1 proponents say the bond would also fund programs specifically designed to help college students, youth exiting foster care, farmworkers, tribal communities and low-income first-time homebuyers.
Notable endorsements: The coalition (https://yesonprop1ca.com/coalition) of Proposition 1 supporters includes the Southern California Association of Nonprofit Housing, the California Association of Veterans Service Agencies and the California Federation of Labor Unions.
Here’s what opponents say
There is no organized campaign against Proposition 1, but a handful of Republican state lawmakers voted against putting it on the ballot. State Sen. Tony Strickland, who represents coastal Orange County and pockets of L.A. County, said Proposition 1 has a “noble goal” but could end up “bankrupting our next generation.” He said, “We could definitely find $10 billion within the general fund spending, and within our normal budget, without doing bond indebtedness.”
Notable opposition: The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a frequent critic of new California revenue proposals, opposes Proposition 1 in its election guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/). The group writes that bonds rely on borrowed money, and debt service costs add up over time. "When used to pay for programs instead of capital projects, it’s a much greater burden on taxpayers than just paying for these programs from the budget," the Howard Jarvis guide says.
Potential financial impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s Office said (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026) repayment of the Proposition 1 bonds would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for the next 25 years.
Because bonds would need to be repaid with interest, the legislative analysis said costs would likely end up about 15% higher than if the state paid for the programs with existing funding.
In total, the analysis said Proposition 1 would provide subsidies for an estimated 40,000 rental apartments, 2,500 farmworker units, 1,200 college student beds and would help up to 40,000 households achieve homeownership, including about 2,100 veterans.

PROP
1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments, nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan. Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
PROPOSAL
New General Obligation Bond for Housing. Proposition 1 allows the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a $10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
State Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides bond funding for various types of housing programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of years. The major categories of housing programs supported by the bond are:
Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings&#46 These programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site service (such as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water, sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for both rental and owner-occupied housing.
Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million, split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for affordable student housing.
Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes. Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs.
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences, condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years . The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds. These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting the production and repair of homes.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no.
